analysis: Palula deec̣híṇu and Shina dac̣híno/daṣínu all accent the final root syllable before the gender ending, although the old adjective is initially accented. The agreement survives different initial-vowel qualities and affricate histories. Because the old later vowel was short, this cannot be explained by attraction to a pre-existing long vowel; it is a diagnostic extended-stem accent case.
unresolved: The western initial ee and precise date of extension remain segmental/chronological questions, not exceptions to the locus pattern.

analysis: Strand ḍʹêṇi ‘shin’ is an early-root-accented feminine derivative, with ee plausibly reflecting i-triggered fronting. Stick/rod to shinbone supplies an independent semantic link. The older Shina handle and shin records are different formations; their quantities and unmarked contours cannot be pooled. Old daṇḍikā gives better morphological support than the bare stick headword.
unresolved: Confirm retroflexion and the timing of root lengthening/umlaut; the extended derivative's historical accent remains reconstructed.

analysis: Kalkoti dit and Palula dito belong to the perfective of give, while Palula díi is the citation for the entire paradigm. Turner explicitly supplies the i-vowel participial alternatives and discusses their analogical history, so a simple a-to-i sound law is inappropriate. The citation is also represented under dádāti 6141; the two old stems are one modern verbal complex.
unresolved: Recover the actual perfective's accent separately from the dictionary citation; unmarked dit does not mean tonelessness.

analysis: Palula díi, bare d-, Kalkoti duun and Kundal di represent different renewed cells of a highly irregular verb. Initial reduplication and old finite morphology are largely lost, so the old third-person accent cannot be projected onto all citations. The perfective requires the separate dattá/dita family.
unresolved: Analyze give by cell, including source-specific tone in Kalkoti, and avoid duplicate family-level confirmations with 6140.

analysis: Palula dáand/Biori dan and the Biori inflected dáanda show old root prominence with different lengthening environments. Short Shina don is fixed in the documented Kohistani don/dódi paradigm, supporting barytone inheritance even when the citation cannot show mora accent. Kalkoti daan is explicitly among the toneless comparisons in Hultman's tone table, making it stronger evidence than an ordinary unmarked glossary item.
unresolved: Keep explicit tone-analysis examples distinct from merely unmarked records; nasal-cluster syllabification and analogy affect Biori lengthening.

analysis: Gilgit dabóon accents the inherited later long vowel early, while the old first vowel is short and accented. This independently expands the short-to-later-long attraction candidate class beyond ‘fire’. The m-to-b and ū-to-oo developments need comparison, and Brokskat damōn is unmarked but supports the general stem shape.
unresolved: Check whether the lord/master formation was inherited unchanged or remodeled; the accent-locus match is stronger than the exact vowel-history claim.

analysis: Gilgit damiǰaár ‘trouble’ is an abstract derived from a suffer/hurt verb, with an accented final -aar formation. The old causative finite verb is not its immediate accentual input. The added inchoative and nominalizing material provide a morphological explanation for final prominence independent of the inherited root.
unresolved: Identify the nominalizer and compare it across other verbs before calling the outcome deterministic.

analysis: Palula dáaš/Biori daš fits later Ashret closed-a lengthening with early accent, while Shina dáai/dái loses the sibilant and forms a vowel/glide sequence. Both preserve initial prominence at the level of the historical root, but their mora counts are not directly equivalent. Kalkoti deeš has an independent front-vowel history requiring comparison with other numerals.
unresolved: Do not force all Shina ai spellings into a doubled-vowel mora category; test numeral-series effects separately.

analysis: Palula daáǰa has a late long root in its citation formation, whereas Shina daǰ- is an unmarked bound stem. The old hy cluster and its contraction can provide a distinct source of length, unlike ordinary open-syllable a lengthening. Kundal dajā̂ is a different suffixed verbal form. These are not matched finite cells.
unresolved: Compare the imperative and finite paradigm and establish whether Palula aa derives from hy contraction or a morphological stem alternation.

input: dā́tra versus independently reconstructed *dātrī and attested dāti
analysis: Astori dáli preserves initial prominence but has shortened the old long vowel and replaced the tr cluster with l. The feminine sickle formation is independently supported by the old entry, so its final i is not an arbitrary rescue suffix. The short modern accent is informative about locus but not early/late mora alignment.
unresolved: The tr-to-l and quantity history require a specific intermediate or contact analysis.

analysis: Gilgit dóono and Guresi dóonu have early root accent before the gender vowel, despite old final accent. This fits a substantivized extended adjective, with the long root retained and rounded in the nasal environment. The old tamed-ox sense independently supports the semantic identification.
unresolved: Distinguish this ox formation from simple cattle nouns and from homophonous don ‘tooth/herd’; the precise extension remains reconstructed.

analysis: Palula dawóo/Biori dawúu has accent in the causative-type citation ending, with p weakening to w. The request/want meaning can arise from causing to give, and the morphology is independently causative in the old source. The ending's early long vowel and dialect raising are a cell-specific outcome, not a simple retained accent on old pā.
unresolved: Compare other causatives to quantify the shared morphology and avoid mixing them with root-accented imperatives.

analysis: Gilgit ẓatáai ‘leather sack’ has early accent on its later long aa after considerable cluster and suffix remodeling. The old -ēya derivative and the leather-container semantics support a relationship, but old first long ā and later ē do not map transparently onto modern vowels. This is not a clean short-to-long attraction case.
unresolved: A closer leather-bag formation and a derivation of the initial affricate are needed before scoring accent history.

analysis: Strand dy- is a consonantal root and older dyūm/dhyūm have finite suffixes. There is no modern root vowel whose accent can be aligned with the old finite form. Variation in aspiration also points to source or morphological differences that must be controlled.
unresolved: No lexical mora prediction can be tested from these citations; compare finite and converb cells explicitly.

analysis: Palula deés and Kohistani deés have late long accent, compatible with final-accent loss after contraction. Gilgit dées/déez, Guresi dées and Astori déez are early, so the same broad old input has a real dialectal split. A different inherited day stem, analogical alignment with a fixed noun class, or earlier accent transfer could explain the early group; none is established by citation alone.
unresolved: Check complete paradigms and old divas/divan alternatives independently rather than positing one exception per dialect.

analysis: Gilgit diš is a short monosyllable with the appropriate place/region sense. It is compatible with old root prominence but cannot distinguish fixed/mobile accent from the citation alone. The consonant is retained much more directly than in dēśá ‘village’, making it useful as a separate related-root control rather than a duplicate.
unresolved: Its inflectional class is the relevant test; do not merge díś with deśá solely to explain the latter's accent.

analysis: Palula dhrígu and Shina ẓígo/j̣ígu have short root accent before the gender vowel, against the old final-accented adjective. Root-final accent assignment explains locus, while old ī shortening before the rg(h) history is independently required. Newer Kalkoti dríg has H associated with final-vowel loss, whereas the older unmarked drig is not itself evidence of no H. Kundal drī̌g is another distinct quantity outcome.
unresolved: The Kundal lie-down phrase is a derivative/construction, and the timing of shortening and r/aspiration movement differs by branch.

analysis: Gilgit duuk is long but unmarked, while older duk is short and has the related debt/guilt sense. This widely circulating Indo-Aryan abstract noun may be inherited or borrowed. Loss of ḥkh and accent on a long vowel cannot be reconstructed from an unmarked headword.
unresolved: Verify source inflection and borrowing stratum before using it in an accent class.

analysis: The main Shina dialects have short dut and Kundal dud after reduction of gdh. This is an important countercontrol to universal compensatory lengthening after old clusters. Old final accent may survive as a mobile inflectional class, but the short citation does not show it. Palula's c̣hiír ‘milk’ belongs to a different etymon.
unresolved: Read inflections and keep the two milk roots separate in cross-language tables.

analysis: Palula dhrúuk/Biori dhráak has early long accent and a striking aa/uu dialect correspondence, despite old short root u and final accent. The gorge/difficult-passage semantics fit well, but simple final-a apocope cannot create that western vowel chain. A remodeled or metathesized long-vowel/diphthongal input is required; r and aspiration movement are only part of the account.
unresolved: Seek an independently supported extended or compound precursor; retain both quantity and early-accent residuals.

input: duhitŕ̥ and its old strong/weak case stems
analysis: Palula dhií and Shina dií/diíh have late accent on a long contracted vowel, with Kundal dī̌ giving a compatible contour notation pending source verification. The old accented final vocalic r and loss of h/t/r provide a plausible right-edge source, but this requires the kinship paradigm rather than a simple CVCá noun rule. Longer daughter forms preserve evidence of the lost consonants or extensions.
unresolved: Reconstruct the particular case stem and contraction order; distinguish primary daughter forms from derived plurals.

input: dūrá and independently accented dūrám/dūrḗ adverbs
analysis: Gilgit duúr is late, compatible with final-accent apocope, whereas Kohistani/Guresi/Astori dúur is early. Palula dhúura retains a final vowel and early root prominence; its adverbial formation may therefore differ. The other Shina dialects remain early even with consonant-final citations, so retained modern endings alone do not explain the whole split. Kalkoti dùúr adds an independent L from aspiration history.
unresolved: Test adjective versus adverb formation and inflection across dialects; aspiration cannot distinguish the main Shina early/late forms.

analysis: Gilgit diši- is a bound derived stem and older dišoiki an infinitive. The i root vowel may reflect a causative/umlaut history rather than regular shortening of ū, and the old blame sense matches speaking ill of someone. Modern suffix accent is not directly comparable to the old finite causative accent.
unresolved: Identify the stem-vowel alternation and matched finite cells; the isolated i source row is a fragment.

analysis: Strand dhrîʹsṭo is an explicitly irregular past form with late long root accent; Kalkoti driṣ and Sauji dərṣo are other perfective reflexes. Palula páaša is the suppletive present/citation and not a phonological reflex of dr̥ṣṭá. The old short vocalic r and modern long ī require a separate stem/quantity history, while final o is morphological.
unresolved: Extract the actual perfective from the Palula paradigm and exclude the suppletive p- citation from direct correspondence counts.

input: dēvŕ̥ / dēvará and explicitly attested dḗvara
analysis: Palula díir/Biori déer and Strand dʹîr have early root accent and the expected early-ee raising correspondence. The old entry explicitly supplies barytone dḗvara, so these are not secure counterexamples based only on final-accented dēvará. Kalkoti däär and Sauji dēro need their own vowel/ending histories and lack reliable tone here.
unresolved: Use a sensitivity analysis over the attested old alternatives rather than selecting the convenient one invisibly.

analysis: Palula díiš/Biori déeš is fixed and early, against final-accented dēśá. Ashret raising proves that root accent was already early before the early-ee-to-ii change, so a late post-raising retraction is not enough. Liljegren explicitly identifies this as an unexplained earlier shift. An analogical relationship to another fixed village/place noun is possible, but requires independent evidence.
unresolved: Retain as a diagnostic early retraction/formation residual; neither short-vowel lengthening nor aspiration explains it.

analysis: Palula dhreég has late long accent, compatible with loss of final old accent after ai-to-ee and cluster remodeling. The light verb in dhreég d- is separate, and the base's sense ‘length’ is an independently appropriate source for lie/stretch out. Compare this late abstract noun with early-root dhrígu ‘long’ to isolate derivational accent from shared segments.
unresolved: The exact dairgha versus dairghya formation needs source control; the contrast should be counted as one related derivational complex.

analysis: Palula dhoóṛ is late long, consistent with right-edge prominence after loss of an old accented ending. The earlier dohóṛ-type form shows that contraction and aspiration movement intervene, so the derivation is more than direct final-a apocope. Night-to-yesterday is a familiar calendrical semantic specialization but must be established for the exact old case form.
unresolved: The ṣ-to-ṛ and temporal suffix history remain to be explained; Kundal dōy is unmarked.

analysis: Biori dhrac̣ and short Shina grape forms support an earlier short root, while Ashret dhráac̣ is early despite aspiration. It is therefore a genuine counterexample to unrestricted aspirated closed-a late lengthening, like ‘mountain’. The old entry's long/short and barytone/oxytone variants cannot alone explain the modern conditioning failure. The compound wild-vine forms have additional feminine morphology.
unresolved: Check whether aspiration or length belonged to a different chronological layer; preserve the alternative old inputs without choosing solely by accent fit.

analysis: Palula bóoš/Biori báaš and Shina báai have early prominence on the old accented long vowel after contraction of the teen compound. Ashret oo raising and main-Shina ai formation are branch-specific segmental developments. This is one of the teens whose old accent independently agrees with the modern series and can serve as a model for analogy in eleven/fourteen/fifteen.
unresolved: The entire series is morphologically related, so individual teens are not fully independent sound-law confirmations.

analysis: Gilgit dugúnyo ‘again’ preserves prominence on the later constituent before an added yo formation. Twice/double to once more is a plausible semantic development, and the old final accent is compatible at the constituent level. The modern suffix and loss of v must be identified before equating vowel positions.
unresolved: This is an adverbial derivative, not an unextended noun apocope test.

analysis: Gilgit dii~ has lost p/n-related segmental material and retains a nasalized long vowel, but the headword is unaccented. The leopard/tiger sense is independently exact enough for cognacy, yet no mora outcome can be inferred from the spelling. The old suffix accent could have survived through contraction, but that remains untested.
unresolved: Use the source paradigm or independently marked citations; do not treat an unmarked long vowel as a neutralized tone.

analysis: Shina don ‘herd’ is short and can preserve a property/cattle sense, while Strand dhʹêni ‘debt’ is an early-root-accented feminine derivative with fronting. The two modern nouns differ in formation and should not share a single outcome cell. Published Kohistani don ‘flock’ has mobile inflection, which would oppose simple preservation of the old barytone class and needs a precise semantic/link check.
unresolved: Confirm the flock/debt etymologies and inflections before invoking a common accent shift.

analysis: Palula dáand/Biori dand is a short-root ridge word with later Ashret early lengthening. Modern aspiration is absent even though older dhān records retain it, so the word cannot be used to test aspirated-onset lengthening without establishing aspiration's timing. The old entry contains both root-accented and final-accented forms, adding input ambiguity.
unresolved: Separate the old stem variants and aspiration loss chronology; do not count modern early aa as proof of one old accent.

analysis: Gilgit daáno ‘bow’ is late on a newly long root before a gender ending, although the main old noun has short root accent. This enlarges the late-long extended-noun class beyond the obvious pt/lp clusters, so a proposed cluster rule must explain the old n/us sequence or admit a morphological quantity source. The alternate old dhanú differs in accent but does not itself supply long ā.
unresolved: Check the bow paradigm and the source of aa; do not broaden compensation to every noun merely to fit this outcome.

analysis: Biori dharáṇ preserves accent on the old medial short vowel after final ī loss. Ashret dharaáṇ is late long in a syllable preceded by unaccented material and aspiration, matching the late closed-a lengthening condition. The locus is retained while the mora alignment is newly created. Kalkoti dä̀rin supplies an independently analyzable low-tone cognate in the newer source.
unresolved: The final ī loss and the source of Kalkoti front vowels are separate; the modern late contour does not imply old oxytone accent.

analysis: Gilgit doó~ ‘roasted grain’ has late long accent and a semantically exact old grain formation. Loss of n and contraction of the two long vowels can leave final prominence, but the modern vowel is a coalesced output rather than an unchanged root ā. Nasalization preserves evidence of the lost consonant.
unresolved: The accent is compatible with the old final prominence; reconstruct the coalescence before using it as a simple long-root apocope count.

analysis: Gilgit dáar preserves early accent on the inherited long root after loss of final ā and aspiration. The ridge/hill meaning is independently included in the old source, so this is a strong semantic and accent retention example. Sauji dhārē has a different ending and unmarked accent.
unresolved: No principal Gilgit accent anomaly; preserve gender/ending distinctions in the western comparison.

analysis: Gilgit dáas has early long accent, compatible with the old root-accented long ā after final material and aspiration are lost. Mountain to uncultivated/desert land is plausible within a topographic field but not perfectly identical. This is supporting retention evidence with a semantic qualification.
unresolved: The late textual attestation and semantic breadth warrant lower confidence than a directly matched basic-vocabulary noun.

analysis: Shina duúm is consistently late long in the major modern sources, matching loss of final accented a after old long ū. Palula dhuumíi instead has an accented final feminine/derived ending and cannot be scored as a different contour on the simple smoke stem. Kundal dùmā̂ contains both low and contour notation in another formation, requiring original-source decoding.
unresolved: Keep simple and feminine smoke nouns separate; the derivative's final accent is not a failure of the simple apocope rule.

analysis: Palula dháama has early root accent in the citation/imperative formation, but its m is not supplied by the old present and may belong to an independently remodeled stem. The eating-satisfaction meaning matches closely, while the older dhāatum finite form suggests a different t-containing base. A one-word retention claim would ignore this stem alternation.
unresolved: Read the full modern paradigm to explain m versus t and its accentual consequences.

analysis: Palula na and Shina na are short negative particles, with Strand marking prominence in a citation. Their accent in a clause can depend on negation type and prosodic context, so the absence of an acute elsewhere is not a lexical innovation. A single short vowel also lacks the long-mora opposition.
unresolved: No lexical mora-accent retention percentage is appropriate; distinguish prohibitive and ordinary negation in context.

analysis: Palula nóong/Biori náang is early and long, with Ashret raising, despite old final accent and short root a. This requires an earlier quantity/accent stage before the raising change, not merely late closed-a lengthening. Loss or reorganization of aspiration and the unexpected nasal-plus-g cluster provide segmental evidence that a remodeled input may be involved. The old geminate alternative alone does not explain early long accent.
unresolved: Reconstruct the nail paradigm and compare the extended nakhara family separately; retain as a substantive residual.

analysis: Gilgit nóoro, Kohistani núuro and Guresi/Astori nóor have early long root accent after contraction of the nakhara stem. Final-root accent assignment in the extended noun and loss of internal kh can account for a common prominence source, with later apocope in some dialects. This is distinct from Palula nóong under nakhá and should not be forced into one segmental rule.
unresolved: The origin of the long rounded vowel and the precise extension are reconstructed; test the contraction against other VkhV sequences.

analysis: Palula náanu and Gilgit náno are root-accented before their gender vowel, agreeing with independently attested barytone nágnaka rather than the simple final-accented adjective. Palula long aa versus Gilgit short a then reflects different quantity history after gn simplification. Sauji niċaṅ requires separate suffix/consonant analysis and is unmarked.
unresolved: This is an unusually well-grounded extension example; the chronology of the modern quantity difference remains separate.
